Well, um, I guess the main reason I finally made the appointment is that I’m just... I’m losing hours of my day. It's really starting to impact my work, my life, everything, really. I'm an engineer, so, you know, being thorough and detail-oriented is part of the job, but this is entirely different. I'm constantly rechecking things. And I mean *constantly*. 

Like, at work, I'll be looking at file dimensions on a project, and I have to check them, and then check them again, and then go through all my revision notes. And I can't just read the notes once or verify the numbers and be done with it. I have to read them, stop, and go back through the exact same sequence. 

But it's not just work, it bleeds into my apartment, too. The door locks are a complete nightmare right now. I'll stand there locking and unlocking, pulling the handle, stepping back, stepping forward. And... and even with my dressing supplies, just checking and rechecking them to make sure they're exactly how they need to be. 

The worst part—the reason it takes up so much time—is that I don’t feel allowed to move on. It’s like my brain won't give me permission to transition to the next task. I just can’t go past it until I’ve gone through the exact same routine enough times. The anxiety just builds up in my chest, and I have to keep doing the routine, repeating the exact same checks, until that feeling finally drops. If I try to walk away before that drop happens, the tension is just unbearable. So I just keep checking, and suddenly an hour or two is just completely gone.

Well, I mean, the thoughts are sort of what drive the whole checking thing in the first place, I guess. It’s not just a blank urge to stand there. There’s a... a very specific, very loud thought track that just cuts right in, no matter what I’m doing. 

Like, with work, I’ll be looking at a CAD file—Computer-Aided Design, you know, for my engineering projects—and I can literally have just finished running a full diagnostic, checked all the load-bearing tolerances, and I *know* I reviewed it properly. I have the data right in front of me on the screen. But then this thought just pushes its way into my head, telling me that I missed one tiny, almost microscopic thing. And it doesn't just stop at 'you made a mistake.' It spirals immediately into this vivid scenario where that one tiny design mistake makes it to manufacturing, the part fails in the real world, and someone gets seriously hurt, or worse, and it will be entirely my fault because I wasn't careful enough. 

And it’s the exact same thing at home with those dressing supplies I mentioned earlier. I have this wound I've been taking care of, and even after I know for an absolute fact that I’ve cleaned the wound area perfectly—like, I’ve used the saline, I’ve applied the ointment exactly how the instructions said, I've done the whole sterile protocol—my brain just starts screaming that I missed one tiny speck of dirt or bacteria. And the thought just loops and loops that it’s going to turn into this massive, severe infection and I'm going to end up in the hospital. 

The most frustrating part of all of this, the thing that makes me feel like I'm losing my grip, is that I know how it sounds. I have a graduate degree. I rely on logic and hard numbers for a living. But when that thought hits, I can’t just reason it away. I try to tell myself, 'You literally just cleaned it, it's fine,' or 'The CAD numbers are right there, you checked them,' but the thought just completely overrides my logic. It just sits there, heavy and terrifying, until I give in and check it all over again.

No, no, they're definitely mine. I mean, I don't hear voices or anything like that, if that's what you're asking. It's not like someone else is beaming them into my head or... or some external force is planting them there. It's entirely my own internal monologue, my own voice in my head.

If I felt like some outside entity was putting these thoughts there, maybe I could just dismiss them as, you know, completely crazy. But because I know it's *my* brain—my highly educated, rational brain that I rely on every single day to do my job—it feels like this massive betrayal. 

It's more like... well, you know how when you're trying to solve a complex problem, your brain naturally generates different scenarios? Like, 'what if X happens, then Y will fail.' That's what my brain is doing, but it's just doing it in absolute overdrive. I've actually spent hours just trying to analyze why I'm doing this to myself. Like, is it a misfiring of my normal risk-assessment skills? Because as an engineer, you're literally trained to look for points of failure. You have to anticipate what could go wrong. So it feels like my own thought process is just taking that professional training and completely weaponizing it against me. 

I'll be sitting there, looking at the screen, and my own inner voice just says, 'Hey, you missed that tolerance.' And I know it's me thinking it. It's just a part of me that absolutely will not shut up. It's my own thoughts, my own voice, just... stuck on this terrifying loop that I can't pause. I really, really wish I could just flip a switch and turn it off, but since it's my own mind, I can't exactly run away from it, can I? It's just there, constantly generating these worst-case scenarios, and I just have to sit there and argue with myself for hours. So, yeah, it's 100% my own thinking. Just... thinking that I have absolutely no control over right now.

No, God no. Not at all. Actually, it’s the exact opposite, and I think that’s why the whole experience is just so incredibly distressing for me. 

You know, as an engineer, we actually take a sort of professional oath. There’s a whole code of ethics, and the very first rule, the paramount thing you learn in grad school, is that you have to hold the safety, health, and welfare of the public above absolutely everything else. That is a core, fundamental value of mine. I take my responsibilities incredibly seriously. I consider myself a highly ethical, caring person. 

So, going back to what I was saying a minute ago about those CAD files... when that thought just violently cuts in, telling me that I missed some microscopic detail and that a design mistake is going to make it to manufacturing and actually hurt someone... it feels completely abhorrent to me. It feels like an attack on the very thing I care most about. It makes me feel like this negligent, dangerous person, which goes completely against everything I know to be true about myself. If I actually didn't care, if I was actually reckless and those were my true values, I wouldn't be spending hours checking my work, right? I'd just send it off and go get a coffee.

And it’s the exact same disconnect with the wound care I brought up. I value logic. I value the scientific method. I know how sterile protocols work, and I believe in empirical facts. But even after I know for an absolute fact that I’ve cleaned the area perfectly, that thought still forces its way in, insisting I missed a tiny speck of dirt and it’s going to turn into a life-threatening infection. It completely contradicts my belief in my own rationality and competence. 

And like I said before, the absolute worst part is that I just can’t reason it away. No matter how much I try to lean on my actual values—my logic, my training, my knowledge that I am a careful, meticulous person—the thoughts just bulldoze right over them. It’s almost like my brain is actively searching for the things I value most, like public safety and my own health and my professional integrity, and it's just holding them hostage. I spend so much time and energy just trying to prove to myself that I'm not the careless monster these thoughts are making me out to be. So, no, they don't align with my values at all. They feel like the exact opposite of who I am.

Well, honestly, it’s... it’s hard to even maintain relationships right now, because I just don't have the time anymore. The checking routines just completely eat up all the time I used to keep for myself, and by extension, for anyone else. 

Like, with work, my project deadlines have actually started slipping, which is terrifying for me given how seriously I take my job. I end up staying late at the office, sometimes hours after everyone else has packed up and gone home, just staring at those CAD files, trying to get comfortable enough to actually submit the work. I just sit there in the quiet office, running the numbers over and over. And because I'm stuck there doing that, or I'm stuck at home doing the whole sterile protocol with the dressing supplies... I've completely dropped off the map socially. 

I used to go to these paddleboarding meetups—there's a group of friends I used to go out on the water with on the weekends, you know, just to decompress and get away from the screens. And I used to do regular workouts, too, which kept me grounded. But I’ve stopped making it to the paddleboarding meetups entirely. I've stopped the workouts. I've stopped pretty much everything. 

My friends will text me, asking where I’ve been or if I want to grab a drink, and what am I supposed to say? I can't exactly tell them I missed the meetup because I spent four hours arguing with myself over a microscopic design flaw that doesn't even exist, or that I couldn't leave my apartment because I was terrified of a speck of dust on my bandage. So I just make up excuses. I tell them I'm swamped with work, which I guess is technically true since I'm staying so late, but it's not the real reason. It's incredibly isolating. You just watch your whole life—your friends, your hobbies, your physical health—just sort of shrink down until there's absolutely nothing left but the checking. So, yeah, it's definitely affecting my friendships, mostly because I'm just not there anymore.

Yeah, it’s... it’s incredibly rigid. It’s not just a quick glance to make sure something is done, it’s an entire production. And that's really the main thing that brings me in here, honestly. I am just losing hours and hours of my day to rechecking things, and it has to be done in this exact, agonizing sequence every single time. 

Like, with work, I don't just look at a drawing and say, 'Okay, looks good.' I have to check the file dimensions first, and then I have to read through the revision notes. Every single one, line by line. And if I get distracted, or if my eyes jump ahead and I look at a revision note before I've fully, 100% verified the dimensions, it doesn't count. I have to start the whole process over from the very beginning. It's like I’m... I just don’t feel allowed to move on. My brain just puts up a wall and says, 'No, that wasn't the right way, you missed a step, do it again.' 

And it’s the exact same thing at home. I mentioned the wound care earlier—when I set out my dressing supplies, they have to be lined up on the bathroom counter in the exact order I’m going to use them. If I accidentally bump the saline bottle, or if I set the medical tape down before the gauze, the whole routine is ruined in my head. I'll actually throw clean supplies away and start over. 

And it's even started bleeding into mundane things now, like the door locks at my apartment. I can't just turn the key and walk to my car like a normal person. I have to turn the deadbolt, push the handle down twice, pull the door toward me with a specific amount of force... and I just repeat that same routine over and over. 

I know exactly how ridiculous it sounds to spend twenty minutes fighting with a door, or hours clicking through the same CAD file, but I just... I can't stop. I have to keep going through the same routine enough times until the anxiety finally drops. I'm literally just standing there, trapped, waiting for this specific feeling of relief, or at least for the panic in my chest to dial back just enough that I feel like I have permission to walk away. If I try to force myself to stop before that feeling hits, the anxiety is just unbearable. I'll make it to my car and have to turn around and go back upstairs. So I just stay there, doing the sequence, over and over, until my brain finally lets me off the hook. It's exhausting. It's just completely taking over my life.

It's honestly... well, it's kind of both. They are entirely wrapped up in each other, because in my head, the mistake is the exact thing that causes the harm, if that makes sense. 

I mean, if you look at work... take the CAD files I was just talking about. I will be sitting there, and I know for a fact I have reviewed the file. I've checked the load tolerances, the material specs, the dimensions, everything. Logically, the rational part of my brain knows I just looked at it and it's fine. What if my knuckle accidentally brushed the sterile side of the gauze pad for half a second? And suddenly I am absolutely convinced that this one tiny oversight is going to turn into a massive, systemic infection. I start picturing going into sepsis, or losing a limb, just completely catastrophic harm to myself. 

So it always starts with the terror of making a mistake, but the weight of it—the reason I get paralyzed—is the harm that mistake will cause to me or to somebody else. And the most frustrating part of all of this, the thing that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that I cannot just reason it away. I'm an engineer. My entire life, my entire graduate education, is built on logic and data and rational deduction. But when that thought cuts in... all my logic just completely evaporates. I can tell myself, "You just cleaned this," or "You just ran the stress simulation," but the "what if" is so incredibly powerful that I just have to go back and do the whole routine all over again. Symmetrical? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I can definitely see why you might ask that, or why someone might assume that, especially with me being an engineer. I think people always just assume engineers want everything perfectly lined up, right angles, you know, perfectly exact and symmetrical on the desk or whatever. So yeah, symmetry doesn't really factor into it at all for me. It's actually kind of funny, my roommate back in grad school was super into keeping our apartment perfectly symmetrical—like the pillows on the couch had to match perfectly on both sides, the chairs had to be equidistant from the table—and that actually used to drive me crazy. So I definitely don't have that going on. My checking is entirely, one hundred percent driven by that terrifying "what if" about the real-world consequences. If I could just leave a file alone knowing it was completely safe and wouldn't hurt anyone, I wouldn't care at all if the visual formatting was a little crooked, you know? It's just the danger aspect. That's the only thing keeping me there.

Yeah, uncertainty is... I mean, that's the whole battle right there. It is absolutely about trying to control that uncertainty, because the feeling of not knowing for sure is just this unbearable, physical weight. But if I try to walk away before that feeling of certainty hits, before the anxiety actually subsides, the panic just spikes so hard I end up running right back to do it all over again. So I just stay there. I just stay trapped, trying to control that uncertainty, trying to force the anxiety down by doing the routine just one more time... and then one more time after that. I just can't move on until my brain gives me permission, and lately, it takes hours to get that permission.

Well, like I was saying just a little bit ago, it's really not about symmetry or making things look exact at all. I know we kind of touched on that, but to really get at what's actually motivating all this... it's strictly these thoughts. It's like my brain just gets completely hijacked.

And it doesn't just stop at "you missed something," it immediately spirals into this absolute, terrifying certainty that this tiny oversight is going to turn into a massive, raging infection, or it's going to be a critical design mistake that actually hurts someone in the real world. And I try... I really, really try to just reason it away. I'll stand there and try to use my engineering brain, try to use logic, like, "You literally just checked the math, you just wiped down the skin, you're fine." But I can't. I just cannot reason it away. The thought is so loud, and so overpowering, and so heavy that all my logic just completely collapses under it. It just loops and loops until I feel like I'm going crazy. 

So, yeah, I really don't care if the bandage is taped on perfectly straight or if the file is formatted exactly right. It's not about exactness. I just care about making that terrifying thought stop, because it just won't leave me alone until I go back and check it all over again.

The distress of hitting 'send' before my brain feels like the file is perfectly checked is somehow worse than the fear of missing a major deadline. Which makes absolutely no logical sense, I know that, but that's what happens. \n\nAnd then the personal side of it... I mean, I've completely stopped making it to the paddleboarding meetups, I've stopped doing my regular workouts... all of it is just gone. And it's all because these routines just entirely eat up the time I used to keep for myself. I used to have a real life, you know? A normal schedule. I'd go to the office, go to the gym, get out on the water on the weekends to clear my head. Now, my entire existence is just going to work, getting trapped at my desk, and then coming home only to get trapped at my front door or in my bathroom with the bandages. The distress isn't just the panic I feel when I'm checking things, it's the... I guess it's the grief of watching my life just shrink. It's shrinking down to absolutely nothing but these routines, and it's just so incredibly depressing to live like this.\n\nDoctor: Are your checking behaviors more about preventing harm to yourself or others, or is it more about avoiding making a mistake?\n\nPatient: It's honestly... well, it's kind of both. They are entirely wrapped up in each other, because in my head, the mistake is the exact thing that causes the harm, if that makes sense. \n\nI mean, if you look at work... take the CAD files I was just talking about. I will be sitting there, and I know for a fact I have reviewed the file. I've checked the load tolerances, the material specs, the dimensions, everything. Logically, the rational part of my brain knows I just looked at it and it's fine. But then this thought just... it just cuts right in. It’s like this loud, blaring alarm bell in my head saying, \"What if you missed one tiny thing? What if you overlooked a single decimal point?\" And the fear isn't just about looking stupid or getting yelled at by my project manager for a typo. It's the terrifying thought that this design mistake is going to get sent to manufacturing, the part is going to be produced, it's going to fail in the field, and it is going to physically hurt someone. Like, someone could actually get injured, or worse, because I didn't check that flange thickness for a twenty-first time. \n\nAnd it is the exact same mechanism with the stuff at home, with the sterile bandages. I know I’ve cleaned the wound area. I literally just watched myself do it. I used the alcohol, I followed the whole protocol. But the second I go to tape it down, that same thought cuts in—what if I missed one microscopic speck of dirt? What if my knuckle accidentally brushed the sterile side of the gauze pad for half a second? And suddenly I am absolutely convinced that this one tiny oversight is going to turn into a massive, systemic infection. I start picturing going into sepsis, or losing a limb, just completely catastrophic harm to myself. \n\nSo it always starts with the terror of making a mistake, but the weight of it—the reason I get paralyzed—is the harm that mistake will cause to me or to somebody else. And the most frustrating part of all of this, the thing that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that I cannot just reason it away. I'm an engineer. My entire life, my entire graduate education, is built on logic and data and rational deduction. But when that thought cuts in... all my logic just completely evaporates. I can tell myself, \"You just cleaned this,\" or \"You just ran the stress simulation,\" but the \"what if\" is so incredibly powerful that I just have to go back and do the whole routine all over again. I just can't reason with it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these checking behaviors have anything to do with making things symmetrical or exact in some way?\n\nPatient: Symmetrical? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I can definitely see why you might ask that, or why someone might assume that, especially with me being an engineer. I think people always just assume engineers want everything perfectly lined up, right angles, you know, perfectly exact and symmetrical on the desk or whatever. But honestly, if you were to look at my actual physical workspace, it's a bit of a mess. I've got coffee cups and loose reference papers everywhere. I really don't care if my pens are parallel to my keyboard, or if the boxes of sterile bandages in my bathroom cabinet are stacked perfectly straight. \n\nIt's never about how things look, or some feeling of a room needing to be perfectly balanced or visually symmetrical. It really just goes right back to what I was saying a minute ago about the catastrophic failure aspect. The exactness I care about is only... well, it's only about the data being correct so the physical part doesn't break. Like, I'm checking the decimals on those CAD files not because I need the numbers to look pretty or symmetrical on the screen, but because if the decimal is wrong, the stress load calculation is wrong, and the thing snaps under pressure in the real world. \n\nSo yeah, symmetry doesn't really factor into it at all for me. It's actually kind of funny, my roommate back in grad school was super into keeping our apartment perfectly symmetrical—like the pillows on the couch had to match perfectly on both sides, the chairs had to be equidistant from the table—and that actually used to drive me crazy. So I definitely don't have that going on. My checking is entirely, one hundred percent driven by that terrifying \"what if\" about the real-world consequences. If I could just leave a file alone knowing it was completely safe and wouldn't hurt anyone, I wouldn't care at all if the visual formatting was a little crooked, you know? It's just the danger aspect. That's the only thing keeping me there.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're trying to control the outcome of events or prevent uncertainty when you engage in these checking behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yeah, uncertainty is... I mean, that's the whole battle right there. It is absolutely about trying to control that uncertainty, because the feeling of not knowing for sure is just this unbearable, physical weight. It’s like I'm trying to build this impenetrable wall against anything going wrong, and the only bricks I have are these routines. \n\nAnd really, that’s exactly what brings me in here to see you. I am just... I'm losing hours and hours of my day to rechecking things. It's not just a quick glance to make sure I locked up. I'm talking about getting completely stuck in these massive loops with my dressing supplies, the door locks at my apartment, the CAD file dimensions I was talking about earlier, even just my basic revision notes on a project. That's really the best way I can describe it. It's like my brain puts up a concrete roadblock, and I am physically not permitted to go to sleep, or leave the office, or finish bandaging my arm until I’ve gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. And it's not even a logical set number, it's just... I have to keep doing it, over and over, checking the lock, checking the sterile packaging, checking the file dimensions, until the anxiety finally drops enough for me to breathe. \n\nIt’s so incredibly exhausting because I know I’m wasting time. I can look at the clock and realize I’ve been standing at the front door jiggling the deadbolt for twenty minutes. But if I try to walk away before that feeling of certainty hits, before the anxiety actually subsides, the panic just spikes so hard I end up running right back to do it all over again. So I just stay there. I just stay trapped, trying to control that uncertainty, trying to force the anxiety down by doing the routine just one more time... and then one more time after that. I just can't move on until my brain gives me permission, and lately, it takes hours to get that permission.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your checking behaviors are an attempt to achieve perfection in your daily tasks or to maintain control over your environment?\n\nPatient: Perfection? No, I... I really wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, when I think of perfection, I think of someone who wants everything to be flawless just for the sake of it being flawless, you know? Like they're striving for some ideal standard or they want to be the absolute best at everything they do. \n\nIf you were to look at my normal daily tasks, the ones that don't trigger this whole cycle, I'm actually pretty careless. Well, maybe not careless, but I definitely don't care about perfection. Like, when I cook dinner, I'm just hacking up vegetables and throwing them in a pan. I don't care if the onions are diced to the exact same millimeter. My laundry is literally just shoved into my dresser drawers. I don't fold my t-shirts into perfect little squares or organize them by color. I just shove them in so the drawer closes. \n\nAnd as for maintaining control over my environment... I mean, my apartment is kind of chaotic, honestly. I think I have two dead lightbulbs in the hallway right now that I haven't bothered to change in over a month. There's junk mail piled up on the kitchen counter. So I'm definitely not trying to master my domain or control every little thing around me. I don't have that need to dictate how everything in my space operates.\n\nIt’s just... it’s really just the danger aspect I was talking about before. The perfection thing, it almost sounds like it would be a choice, right? Like a preference. Like, \"Oh, I prefer my work to be perfect, I prefer my house to be perfectly controlled.\" But this isn't a preference. I don't *want* to be standing at the door checking the lock. I don't *want* to be staring at the sterile gauze until my eyes cross. It’s not because I want the bandage to be applied perfectly, it's because I'm absolutely terrified of the infection. \n\nSo, yeah, it's definitely not about being perfect or controlling my environment. If I could just exist in a totally messy, completely uncontrolled environment without that constant, screaming feeling that someone was going to die or I was going to lose an arm because I didn't check a lock or a load tolerance, I would be thrilled. I would absolutely love to just let things be imperfect. I just... I don't have that luxury when my brain is telling me that a mistake means a catastrophe.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your checking behaviors are motivated by a desire to make things symmetrical or exact?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying just a little bit ago, it's really not about symmetry or making things look exact at all. I know this sounds a lot like what we were just trying to unpack a second ago, and I really want to give you a straight answer on the whole consequence thing, the harm aspect. But it is just... it is like my brain does not even get that far down the timeline, if that makes sense? I mean, I think we're kind of just circling back to the exact same thing we were just talking about, right? The whole mistakes versus control thing. I... I really don't know how to separate those two concepts, especially not in the way you're asking, where it's like, is it *primarily* this or *primarily* that.

Symmetrical or exact... well, exactness is obviously a huge part of engineering. You have to be exact with your math. But when we are talking about these checking loops, it is not really about making things look perfectly balanced or symmetrical. I am not lining up my pens or making sure my shoes are perfectly parallel in the closet or anything like that. 

What actually brings me in to see you, the thing that is really tearing my life apart right now, is that I am losing hours and hours to just rechecking things. And I mean literally losing hours out of my day. I will get stuck on my dressing supplies for my arm, or the door locks, or the file dimensions on my screen, or my revision notes for a project. And it is not because I want the revision notes to look pretty or symmetrical. It is because I physically do not feel allowed to move on. 

It is like there is this invisible wall in my head, and I have to go through the exact same routine, checking the lock, checking the files, checking the bandages, over and over again. I cannot transition to the next part of my day or the next task at work until I have gone through that routine enough times that the anxiety finally drops. I am just standing there, waiting for this specific internal signal, this release of pressure, that tells me I have done it enough. 

If I try to walk away before that anxiety drops, the panic just pulls me right back to the door or the desk. I will tell myself I can just leave, but my body will not let me. So I guess the routine itself has to be executed a certain way, but it is not driven by a need for visual symmetry or exactness in the environment. It is entirely driven by just waiting for that awful feeling to subside so I am finally allowed to go on with my life.
